resources.string: Marine submerged flowering plants with creeping rhizomes and ribbon-like leaves; flowers occur on flattened spadices.
Monocot herbs, often rhizomatous or bulbous, with sword-like leaves and flowers of three sepals and three petals.
An ancient gymnosperm family represented by Welwitschia, a desert plant with two persistent leaves and separate male and female cones.
Living horsetails are rhizomatous plants with jointed, ribbed stems and terminal spore-bearing strobili; they have no flowers or seeds.
Carnivorous tropical vines with leaf-tip tendrils ending in fluid-filled pitfall pitchers; flowers are small and unisexual.

A cane-forming shrub or small tree with ringed stems and dense terminal tufts of arching, strap-like leaves. Branched clusters of white, pink-striped flowers are intensely fragrant, especially at night; orange-red berries follow.
Habit: branched cane with terminal leaf tufts
Flower: fragrant white flower with pink lines

A minute free-floating aquatic plant made of one or several flat oval fronds, each usually bearing a single dangling root. Tiny flowers are rarely produced; the plant most often spreads by budding daughter fronds.
Quiet, nutrient-rich fresh waters across much of the temperate world; widely distributed.

A fully submerged marine flowering plant, not a seaweed. Long ribbon-like leaves arise from a creeping rhizome rooted in sediment. Reproductive shoots carry a flattened spadix enclosed by a sheath, with alternating male and female flowers; fruits are small nutlets.
Temperate marine coasts of the Northern Hemisphere, rooted in shallow sandy or muddy seabeds.

A rhizomatous wetland perennial with upright sword-shaped leaves arranged in fans. The large yellow iris flowers have three broad, downward-spreading outer tepals marked by fine brown-purple veins and three smaller inner tepals. Capsules contain many flattened seeds. Rhizomes and other tissues are poisonous; the species can be invasive outside its native range.
Native through Europe, western Asia and north-western Africa; naturalised and invasive in some regions beyond its range.
Fan of sword-shaped leaves and rhizome
Yellow flower with veined outer tepals

A stemless or nearly stemless yucca forming loose colonies of pale blue-green rosettes. The stiff leaves are narrow and toothed with small marginal prickles; an erect branched panicle bears pale bell-shaped flowers, followed by dry capsules.
Native to north-central Texas in the United States, on limestone prairie and rocky soils.
Colony of pale rosettes with flower stalk
Glaucous leaf with tiny marginal teeth

A much-branched evergreen shrub or small tree with slender cane-like stems and short, narrow leaves clustered toward shoot tips. The leaves commonly angle or curve back from the stem. Small fragrant flowers occur in terminal panicles and are followed by rounded orange to red berries. Leaf form varies among accepted varieties.
Native to north-eastern Mozambique and western Indian Ocean islands, including Madagascar, Mauritius and Réunion.
Branched shrub with leafy shoot tips

A very large rhizomatous herb whose apparent trunk is a pseudostem of overlapping leaf sheaths. Broad leaves tear readily along their parallel veins. The pendant inflorescence has large dark bracts; fruits are angular and filled with hard black seeds, unlike the mostly seedless cultivated dessert bananas.
Native from tropical South and Southeast Asia through southern China; cultivated and naturalised in warmer regions.

A massive solitary palm with a stout trunk patterned by diamond-shaped leaf-base scars and a crown of arching pinnate fronds. Leaflets are narrow and stiff, with sharp basal spines. Branched inflorescences emerge among the leaves; female plants produce clusters of orange date-like drupes, generally smaller and less fleshy than dates of Phoenix dactylifera.
Endemic to the Canary Islands; widely planted in warm regions.
Solitary palm with scarred trunk and crown
Pinnate frond with sharp basal spines

A tall, straight-trunked pine with an open crown in maturity. Soft slender needles occur in bundles of five and have fine white stomatal lines. Long, narrow, slightly curved seed cones hang from branches; pollen cones form clusters near shoot bases.
Eastern North America, from Newfoundland and the Great Lakes region south through the Appalachians.

A short, slow-growing, often multi-trunked pine with a broad irregular crown. Stout needles are borne in pairs and persist for several years. Rounded seed cones mature over two seasons and release large edible pine nuts; cone crops vary greatly from year to year.
Native to the Colorado Plateau and adjacent dry uplands of the south-western United States.

A tall evergreen conifer with a straight trunk, conical crown and distinctly drooping branchlets. Sharp four-sided needles attach singly around the twig on small woody pegs. Long cylindrical seed cones hang downward and fall intact after releasing winged seeds.
Native to northern and central Europe, with natural range extending into the Alps and western Russia.

A deciduous conifer with an open, tiered crown and short spur shoots. Soft needles are borne singly on long shoots but in dense rosettes on short shoots, turning golden before falling in autumn. Small female cones stand upright on branches and persist after opening.
Native to the Alps and other central European mountain ranges; planted widely elsewhere.
Open tiered tree with needle rosettes
Needles clustered on a short shoot

A very tall evergreen conifer with a straight trunk and conical crown, becoming broader with age. Flattened, soft needles attach singly around the twig. The pendant seed cone is distinctive for long three-pointed bracts that protrude beyond its scales.
Western North America, from British Columbia to California and the Rocky Mountains.

A large deciduous conifer with a swollen, fluted or buttressed trunk and fine feathery shoots. Flat linear leaves are arranged in two ranks and fall in autumn. Trees in or near water may form woody upward-growing root knees (pneumatophores). Rounded seed cones and slender pollen-cone clusters are separate reproductive structures.
Native to the south-eastern and east-central United States and parts of Mexico and Guatemala, especially floodplains and swamps.
Deciduous conifer with buttressed base and knees

A giant clump-forming tropical bamboo with short pachymorph rhizomes and exceptionally tall, thick, hollow culms divided by prominent nodes. Branches and large lanceolate leaves are concentrated higher on the culms. The inconspicuous flowers are grass spikelets and flowering is infrequent; fruit is a caryopsis.
Native from eastern India and the eastern Himalaya to southern China and mainland Southeast Asia.
Broad lanceolate blade with parallel veins

A giant high-Andean bromeliad forming a dense rosette of stiff, sharply spined leaves. After many decades it sends up a massive branched inflorescence several metres tall, flowers once, sets capsules and dies (monocarpic). Its unusually delayed flowering and restricted high-elevation habitat make it vulnerable to disturbance.
High-Andean puna of Peru and Bolivia.
Giant spiny rosette with towering flowering spike
Rigid leaf with sharp marginal spines

A large terrestrial bromeliad with a dense rosette of long, stiff, grey-green leaves edged by strong recurved spines. The branched flowering stalk bears greenish-yellow tubular flowers with three sepals and three petals; dry capsules contain seeds. The hooked spines can entangle animals, though reports of animal trapping are anecdotal and should not be treated as a reliable diagnostic trait.
Central Chile, mainly coastal and seasonally dry scrub.
Spiny rosette and tall flowering stalk

An exceptionally long-lived gymnosperm with a short, woody, unbranched trunk and only two persistent strap-shaped leaves. The leaves continue growing from their bases and split into ragged ribbons at their ends. Male and female reproductive cones occur on separate plants; it has no flowers or true fruits.
Arid fog-desert of south-western Angola and north-western Namibia.
Short trunk bearing two long ribbon leaves
Broad strap leaf splitting into ribbons

A rhizomatous spore-bearing plant with hollow, ribbed, jointed green stems. Sterile shoots carry whorls of slender branches at the nodes; fertile shoots bear a terminal strobilus of sporangia and are generally unbranched. It has no flowers, seeds or fruits. The species contains toxic alkaloids and is a livestock hazard in contaminated forage.
Temperate Northern Hemisphere, especially marshes, wet meadows and fens.
Jointed shoots with whorled branches and strobilus
Sheath teeth at a stem node

A terrestrial carnivorous pitcher plant with a scrambling stem and leathery leaves whose tendrils terminate in large urn-shaped traps. The lower pitchers may hold several litres; a ridged, toothed peristome surrounds the opening and a lid bears nectar glands beneath. Its flowers are small and borne in a raceme; the species is endangered and listed in CITES Appendix I.
Endemic to high-elevation sites on Mount Kinabalu and Mount Tambuyukon, Sabah, Borneo.
Terrestrial rosette with large ground pitchers
Urn-shaped pitcher with lid and ribbed lip

Selected plant lineages from marine meadows and temperate forests to deserts and tropical mountains.
